extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, adjudicators, War Department officials, and legal researchers concerned with volunteer army musters, discharges, and laws of war
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and administrative rules governing muster-out, retention, discharge, record alteration, and related doctrines in the volunteer army, plus definitions and key rules of the laws of war (spies, prisoners, property, press, nonintercourse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent volunteers held mustered out at organization's muster-out date
rubrics_metrics.description: General Orders Nos. 108 of 1863, 124 of 1898, and 13 of 1899 fix the general policy that Volunteers who are absent at the date of muster out of their organizations shall be held to have been mustered out at the date of muster out of the organization to which they belonged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent without leave (AWOL) at muster-out becomes civilian; discharge not later effective
rubrics_metrics.description: A Volunteer soldier absent without leave at the time his regiment was mustered out and the Volunteer forces were disbanded became a civilian and, being no longer in the service, could not later be discharged; a certificate to that effect may be given by the War Department.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prisoner of war at muster-out considered in service until return and designated report date
rubrics_metrics.description: Under General Orders No. 108 (1863) soldiers who were prisoners of war when their company was mustered out were to 'be considered as in the service until their arrival in a loyal State, with an allowance of time necessary for their return to their respective places of enrollment.' A soldier who was POW at muster out but, after release, furloughed and ordered to report at a post on a certain date was in service until that designated date and considered mustered out on that date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of office: occupant reverts to citizen; no muster out necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: When an office (e.g., supernumerary second lieutenant) was abolished by statute, the occupant reverted to the status of citizen and no muster out was necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dropped-from-rolls deserters not mustered out with organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteers who had been dropped from the rolls as deserters before the muster out of their organizations were not mustered out at the organization's muster-out date but were separated from the service by operation of being dropped from the rolls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge effective date when held in service after organization muster-out
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Volunteer soldier was held in the service by proper authority after the muster out of his organization, his discharge takes effect on the date when he receives notice that he has been discharged; but if he was not held in service by proper authority his discharge takes effect on the date of the muster out of the organization to which he belonged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer retained and ordered to report by letter considered in service until receipt of discharge order
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer retained in service after his command was mustered out and ordered by The Adjutant General (or other competent authority) to proceed home and report by letter to The Adjutant General for discharge must be considered in service until he received the order for his discharge, or, if it cannot be ascertained when he received notice, until the date of the order directing discharge, provided he obeyed the order without delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retained and ordered to report to chief mustering officer considered in service until issue of discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer or enlisted man retained in service after the muster out of his command and subsequently ordered to report to the chief mustering officer of his State for discharge must be considered in service until the date of the issue of that discharge, provided he obeyed and reported without delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary withdrawal or failure to obey orders separates service at date of withdrawal or last official act
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer or enlisted man retained in service or subjected to military control after muster out who voluntarily withdrew himself from such service or control without permission, or who failed to promptly obey an order to proceed to his home and report, must be considered separated from the service on the date he withdrew or was relieved from duty; if that date is not ascertainable, service is considered terminated on the date of the last official order issued or last official act done while still actually rendering military service or under military control.

rubrics_metrics.name: No nunc pro tunc muster-out; status cannot be retroactively created
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no such thing as a man's being mustered out from the military service nunc pro tunc any more than a man can die nunc pro tunc. A soldier must remain a soldier until he changes to the status of civilian; one cannot by order create a fact to-day and carry it back to a prior date to set it up as a fact occurring on that date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer retained for court-martial may not be mustered out as of date prior to trial
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer retained in the service after his organization was mustered out for the purpose of trial by court-martial may not be mustered out as of a date previous to the trial; where acquitted he may not be mustered out as of a date prior to the proceedings of the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: After volunteer army passes out, no authority to change muster-out records
rubrics_metrics.description: After a Volunteer Army has passed out of existence there is no authority of law under which the War Department can change the record of muster out of a soldier so as to make it appear otherwise than as shown by the official records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer mustered out with the rank actually held in office, not by duties performed
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer will be mustered out with the rank which he actually has in connection with the office into which he has been mustered, and he cannot be mustered out with a certain grade simply because he is performing the duties of an officer of that grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal muster-out generally irrevocable, except when procured by fraud/misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal muster out of service of an officer cannot be revoked while the volunteer army was in existence unless the muster out was secured by fraud, misrepresentation, or withholding evidence; such fraudulent muster-outs were revocable while the volunteer army existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud vitiates muster-out; government remedies prior to army dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Because fraud vitiates any compact, in cases of fraudulent muster out the Government may elect to treat the mustering out order as of no effect; or it may revoke it, or discharge without honor or dismiss the officer, or order him to be tried by court-martial for his offense at any time preceding the passing out of existence of the volunteer army to which the officer belonged.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department is custodian; may not alter original records without legal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department (Adjutant General's office) is merely the custodian of the records of disbanded volunteer organizations and should not alter or amend the original records in its custody to make them show what it may now think they ought to have shown originally; alteration requires express provision of law. If evidence convinces the reporting officer that the record is incorrect, he may state the record as shown and add a remark showing what he thinks the correct record should be and where evidence may be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: C. 9170; Secretary of War decision under date Mar. 2, 1889 (footnote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Records of 'service not honest and faithful' under Gen. Orders No.13 and Army Reg. 148 are conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: By General Orders No. 13 (Adjutant General's office, 1899) paragraph 148, Army Regulations was extended to volunteer officers; section 3 provides a means of determining whether service has been honest and faithful. When under these regulations a board is appointed its approved finding should be held conclusive, as should the decision of the commanding officer when no board has been appointed or applied for. Records of 'service not honest and faithful' made at discharge under these provisions will be held conclusive and cancellation/alteration/ amendment will be denied regardless of supporting testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: C. 6408 (May 1899); footnote notes War Department concurrence and directive to deny applications to change such records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of war: state prosecuting national right by force; formal declaration not required
rubrics_metrics.description: War is that state in which a nation prosecutes its right by force. Parties belligerent in a war are independent nations, but it is not necessary to constitute war that both parties be acknowledged as independent nations or sovereign States; a state of actual war may exist without any formal declaration by either party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of wars: perfect, imperfect, civil, mixed, Indian
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect war disturbs national peace and lays foundation for all hostility. An imperfect war interrupts peace only in particulars (e.g., reprisals). A civil war is a war de facto within borders of a State. A mixed war is between a nation and private individuals. Active hostilities with Indians do not necessarily constitute a foreign war; no formal declaration required for an Indian war if hostilities exist and military operations carried on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: C. 7721; C. 20570 (Nov. 27, 1906) on Indian hostilities; further authorities cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of war: nonintercourse—commercial intercourse between belligerents interdicted
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental principle of the law of war is that, during a state of war, all commercial intercourse between the belligerents is interdicted and made illegal except when and where it may be expressly authorized by the Government; during the Civil War such trade or intercourse was necessarily suspended unless specially permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: R. 11, 533; 12, 259; others; acts of Congress (July 13, 1861) and presidential proclamations noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonintercourse rule applications: surveillance, aliens, newspapers in occupied territory
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of nonintercourse allows civilians to be put under surveillance, applies to aliens, and is enforceable as to newspapers in occupied territory; violation of the rule is not necessarily the offense of spy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and rulings cited: R. 3, 255 (July 1863); further discussion in R. 9, 95; R. 12, 259 (Jan. 1865).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spies: must be taken in flagrante; disguise/treachery are gravamen; presumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A spy must be taken in flagrante delicto; if he succeeds in returning to his own army the crime does not follow him. The gravamen of being a spy is the treachery or deception practiced—the being in disguise or acting under false pretenses. An enemy officer or soldier discovered lurking disguised in or near a camp in enemy dress is prima facie a spy and liable to trial as such; a disguised enemy who returns to his army cannot properly be tried as spy when later captured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: R. 5, 248; R. 14, 679; C. 21529; citations to statutes (section 1343 R.S.) and Hague Convention references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander in occupied territory may suppress newspapers injurious to public interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The commander of an army in occupation and government of the enemy's country has authority to suppress a newspaper or other publication deemed by him injurious to public interests in exciting opposition to the dominant authority or encouraging support of the enemy's cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharpening of sabers not a violation of laws of war
rubrics_metrics.description: The sharpening of sabers is not a violation of the laws of war nor of the conventions accepted by the United States governing military forces in actual military operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captured and destroyed property rules: title, disposition, compensation principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Destruction of property in battle must be borne by the sufferers; any compensation is bounty rather than a right. Captured property: title accrues to the United States and it may be disposed of only by Congress; a civilian cannot convert captured property to own use; there is no prize money in the Army; personal appropriation of property is a military offense; disposition of recaptured property (of loyal owner, regimental flags) and immovable property rules noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion and authorities appear throughout 'As to property' section (pages cited around 1059–1062); see Prize Cases and other citations.
